Press release translation services: reach media in new markets

October 31, 2023
Communication | Localisation | Marketing

Press release translation is the adaptation of a news announcement into another language, so journalists, editors and customers in that market can read it, trust it and publish it.

A press release is a short document that informs the media and the public about a company event, such as a launch, a partnership, a funding round or a new product.

If your news is only available in English, you limit it to English-speaking newsrooms.

A translated release lets you reach international trade press, regional media and customers in their own language, at the moment the news breaks.

Why do you need press release translation services?

Journalists work to tight deadlines, and most will not translate your release themselves.

If they can copy, adapt and publish a clear version in their own language, your news is far more likely to make it into print or online.

A translated release also shows the market that you take it seriously.

It tells editors and customers that you communicate clearly in their language, which supports your reputation before you have even spoken to them.

Translation matters most when you launch in a new country, announce an international partnership, open an office abroad or manage a crisis that affects customers in several markets.

What makes a press release translation different

A press release follows a strict format, and a good translation respects it while adapting the content for the new audience.

The five questions every release must answer

A well-written release answers who, what, when, where and why in the first paragraphs.

Your translator checks that each answer is clear in the target language, because a reader should understand the news from the headline and opening lines alone.

  • Who: the organisations and people involved, with names and titles spelled consistently.
  • What: the news itself, stated plainly in the headline and first paragraph.
  • When: the date, the time and any embargo, written in the format the local media use.
  • Where: the location or market the news applies to.
  • Why: the reason the news matters and the benefit for the reader.

Localisation, not literal translation

Faithful translation is not the same as literal translation.

The translator keeps your meaning and adapts everything around it, including tone, idioms, date formats, currencies, units of measurement, quotations and contact details.

For example, a UK release dated 4 November uses a day-month-year order that a reader in the United States may misread, and a pound figure may need to be shown in euros for a European newsroom.

This localisation step makes the release read as if it was written in the target language from the start.

Headlines, quotes and boilerplate

Headlines carry the most weight, and they rarely survive word-for-word translation.

Quotes from your spokespeople need to sound natural and keep the speaker's intent, and your company boilerplate must use the same wording on every release.

Brand names, product names and trademarks need a clear instruction on whether to translate them or leave them in English.

How to make your translated release publishable

  • Send the final, approved English version, so translators do not work on a draft that later changes.
  • Share a glossary of product names, job titles and key terms.
  • Tell your translator which countries and publications you are targeting.
  • Give local contact details, including a spokesperson who can answer journalists in that language.
  • Agree the publication date and time across time zones, so every version goes out together.

Publishing your release online

Once the translation is approved, publish each version on a language-specific page of your website's newsroom as well as sending it to the media.

Use the words people search for in that market in the headline and opening paragraph, so journalists and customers can find the news through search.

Keep the same facts, figures and quotes in every language version, so no market receives a different story.

Why quality and timing both matter

News loses value quickly, so a delayed translation can cost you coverage.

An error in a translated release costs more, because a wrong figure, date or name travels with your brand once a journalist publishes it.

That is why professional translation, review by a second linguist and clear deadlines matter more than speed alone.

BeTranslated's professional translators work to your agreed schedule, so that your releases are ready in every language on the day you publish.

You can see how turnaround works for different project types.

Press release translation for your industry

Different sectors have different rules and vocabulary.

A financial announcement needs precise terminology and cautious wording, a product launch needs persuasive copy, and a medical release needs accurate technical language.

BeTranslated assigns linguists who know your sector, and you can explore related specialisations such as marketing, business and finance, technical and legal translation.

Common language pairs for UK companies include French, German, Spanish, Italian, Dutch and Portuguese.

Get your press release translated

Send your release, the languages you need and your publication date, and BeTranslated will quote the project individually.

Rates are quoted per project, based on length, languages and subject.

Request a free, no-obligation quote to get started.

Frequently asked questions

What is press release translation?

It is the translation and localisation of a news announcement into another language. The translator keeps the press release format and adapts tone, dates, currencies and quotes for the target audience.

Why should you translate a press release?

Translation lets you reach journalists and customers who do not read English. Editors are more likely to publish a ready-to-use release in their own language than to translate one themselves.

Can you use machine translation for a press release?

A machine can give you a quick draft, but it can miss tone, idiom and local conventions. Because a press release is public and tied to your brand, a professional translator should review or produce the final text.

What should you send a translator with your release?

Send the final approved version, a glossary of product and company terms, and the target countries and publications. Add the publication date and any embargo time, so the translator can plan the schedule.

Can a translated release go out at the same time as the English one?

Yes, if you plan ahead. Share the final text in advance and agree a delivery date before the embargo, so every language version can be released together.
